mcqs.question: What question is every ILP technique (superscalar, out-of-order, VLIW) fundamentally trying to answer?
options: Which instructions in a single sequential stream are independent enough to execute at the same time
How to increase the clock frequency of the processor
How to reduce the number of transistors used per core
How to compress the instruction encoding to save memory bandwidth
mcqs.explanation: ILP is about extracting parallelism from one instruction stream, which requires identifying which instructions don't depend on each other. Clock frequency, transistor count, and encoding density are separate microarchitecture/ISA concerns, not what ILP techniques target.

mcqs.question: Why are WAR and WAW hazards called 'name dependences' rather than true dependences?
options: Because they only occur in instructions that have literal string names in assembly
Because no value actually flows between the two instructions — they only conflict because they happen to reuse the same register name, which renaming can eliminate
Because they are named after the two engineers who discovered them
Because they only affect floating-point registers, never integer registers
mcqs.explanation: WAR/WAW hazards are artifacts of limited register naming, not genuine data flow — give the second instruction a different physical register and the conflict disappears, which is exactly what register renaming does. RAW is the only dependence where a real value must pass between instructions.

mcqs.question: In a dependence graph, what actually determines the minimum execution time of a sequence, rather than the total instruction count?
options: The number of registers used across all instructions
The total number of independent instructions available
The longest chain of true dependences (the critical path) through the graph
The order in which instructions appear in the source file
mcqs.explanation: Independent instructions can overlap freely, so they don't add to the floor on execution time — only the longest RAW dependence chain (critical path) forces sequential execution and sets the real lower bound, regardless of how many instructions exist overall.
